Messages.Author: Chris Shorb & Tammy Martin
Messages.Body:
What is the most powerful discipline? Why?

What is the weakest discipline? Why?

Which discipline do you find yourself playing the most? (not
necessarily the same as the first thing). Why?

As I was writing these questions, I realized that the 7 new
disciplines (chi, nec, ser, qui, dem, obt, and vis) are by and large
outclassed by the original set. So I think I will limit this to the
original set...

Chris

Messages.Author: mgre...@my-deja.com
Messages.Body:
In article <38A24F55...@alumni.williams.edu>,

shr...@alumni.williams.edu wrote:
> What is the most powerful discipline? Why?
>

Fortitude. Freak Drive/Day Op./Force of Will/Skin of Steel. 4 Amazing
cards and they all do something totally different. Completely versitile
in terms of combat/non-combat and the vampires that have fortitude have
other strong skills too. It requires no other skills to back it up or
make it good. No contest, head and shoulders over the rest.

> What is the weakest discipline? Why?
>

Thaumaturgy. Before the tremere bunnies jump all over me consider that
it is mostly comprised of combat cards that are very bad/unplayable.
Does nothing to stop S:CE or IG and the non-combat cards are mostly
irrelevent. Maybe Magic of the smith is OK. maybe. Tremere and Tremere!
have auspex (Yeah!! violence!! get into combat and..urm..steal 2
blood?, oh... OK I'll take 5 and have my arms torn off then...) and
dominate, which admittedly is a real beating, but is not backed up
in this case with either a) a stealth skill, or b) a combat skill.
Dominate requires one or the other to get it's max. potential. As the
tremere become weaker due to their card base, their primary skill gets
weaker by association. Shotgun Ritual sucks too.

> Which discipline do you find yourself playing the most? (not
> necessarily the same as the first thing). Why?
>

Obfuscate. Because it is the most useful 'couple' skill. If your deck
has a few key actions to perform you have look at playing with the black
boxes. On its own it is not that powerful in that it can't achieve much
and if your actions are in no danger of getting blocked they clog up
your hand. However, if you couple it with game-wrecking actions like
votes, or ally employment, or a Tempation, or massive bleeds then it's
damn fine. It also has the option of some good tricks like Behind You
and Disguised Weapon too.

> As I was writing these questions, I realized that the 7 new
> disciplines (chi, nec, ser, qui, dem, obt, and vis) are by and large
> outclassed by the original set. So I think I will limit this to the
> original set...
>

They are hamstrung by a lack of vampires to use them to the full
potential. Particularly Obt, which could be very good indeed. On the
other hand qui really is pointless.

matt.

> What is the most powerful discipline? Why?

For me it's Presence. It can vote, bleed, and dodge/SCE all with one
discipline. It's easily the most versatile, and options are what I
highly value.

> What is the weakest discipline? Why?

Of the original set, I'm going to have to say that Animalism is the
weakest? Why? There isn't one thing that it does real well...unlike
the other skills.

Presence - Voting
Dominate - Bleeding
Obfuscate - Stealth
Fortitude - Prevent damage and unblockable actions
Potence - Heavy hitting combat with IG
Celerity - You can control combat with this skill if played right.
Auspex - Intercept
Thaumaturgy - Denial (of blood, actions, strikes, etc.)
Animalism - ummm, I guess they untap a lot....

> Which discipline do you find yourself playing the most? (not
> necessarily the same as the first thing). Why?

Celerity. We love combat in Austin, and this is bar none the best
combat skill in the game.

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 09 Feb 2000 21:40:37 -0800, Chris Shorb & Tammy Martin
<shr...@alumni.williams.edu> wrote:

>What is the most powerful discipline? Why?

Dominate. It bleeds. At stealth if necessary (Bonding, Dominate
Kine). It bounces bleeds (Deflection, Redirection). It blood-gains
(Govern at superior). It provides unblockability (Seduction, Sleeping
Mind). It defends against voting (Kindred Coercion, Pulling Strings).
It steals locations (Kine Dominance). It steals retainers (Far
Mastery). It steals vampires (Mind Rape, Grave Robbing). It is
combat defense (Obedience). And you can get it at superior on two
different 4-cap vampires, at inferior on two different 2-cap vampires,
and there are a LOT of 3-caps and 4-caps with inferior.

No other discipline can do anywhere NEAR this much as effectively.

>What is the weakest discipline? Why?

Taken all by itself, you mean? Probably THA. Lots of combat, but
REQUIRES disciplineless cards to function properly (trap or dead-end
alley) and still doesn't quite get the job done. PRE is almost as
good as DOM. FOR is obviously strong. ANI can be pretty nasty at
superior if done right. AUS will stop everything. OBF will get AWAY
with everything, and well-done Night Moves decks are pretty fearsome.
POT is evil. CEL is an excellent support discipline. PRO is quite a
toolbox itself.

>Which discipline do you find yourself playing the most? (not
>necessarily the same as the first thing). Why?

Difficult to answer that... but probably POT, THA, CEL, PRO in that
order. I like beating things up. =)

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
On Thu, 10 Feb 2000, Todd Banister wrote:
> >On the other hand qui really is pointless.
>
> Huh? Please explain.

To some extent, I see what Matt's saying.

Gangrel can stop dodges with Scorpion Sting, and S:CE with Dog Pack (slow
and crap, but what are you gonna do) and Protean can mix with Potence
reasonably easily - since hand strikes and claws mesh well.

Potence has IG (so usable with the above) to stop S:CE and Dodge, weapon
strikes etc.

Animalism can stop maneuvering, weapons etc.

Protean is a supremely useful discipline - it can be offensive (claws,
body flare) and be a back up discipline (lots of maneuvers, lots of
presses etc.).

Quietus, in some respects, suffers in the same way as Thaumaturgy. The
disciplines it lines up with, in V:TES terms, aren't great. You can't
stop S:CE or Dodge with it, except with Hidden Lurker. And once that
becomes obvious, blocking dries up and Assamites don't have a good way to
punish that (e.g. bruise and bleed).

It can, and has been, used well. It's just one of the combat disciplines
that's easiest to scupper - like Thaumaturgy, without some serious work
(e.g. Xian's potence-thaumaturgy deck).

And Quietus doesn't have the luxury of mixing and matching with odd
disciplines, because of so few vampires having it naturally. :(

--

James Coupe

>most siturations. A light sprinkling of Auspex is wonderful, but if you
>created a deck based on it. I imagine it would suffer from hand jam

I object! =) Auspex has Pulse, to bleed. And if you start stopping
EVERYTHING that happens around you, you may discover that your prey's
deck grinds to a miserable halt, and your predator is forced to take
it on the defensive for awhile. Now the trick is figuring out how to
OUST your prey. But Auspex is probably the best 'defensive'
discipline.

It intercepts (easily), which shuts down votes
It bleed bounces (tel. misdirection, which is dual w/intercept)
It bleed reduces (tel. counter... nasty nasty card)
It has some combat toys (aura reading, read intentions, primal
instincts)

Its biggest weakness is that it doesn't have much to SURVIVE combat.
But against the focussed heavy-bleed, monster-vote, oust-quickly
decks, it absolutely wipes the floor with them. The stock
Govern+Bonding bleed looks kinda silly when someone dumps a pair of
Telepathic Counters on it.

Nice little survey, I'll make a few quick answers that you've probably
already seen.

>What is the most powerful discipline? Why?

Dominate & Presence (Tied).
Not only do they both have the capability of a 3+ bleed by weenies
but they also have versatility (Steal, Bounce, S:CE, etc..)

>What is the weakest discipline? Why?

I'm going to buck the trend and say CELERITY.
It unargueably excellent in combat, full of Maneuvers, Press, Dodge,
Addtional Strike, and so on. All the other disciplines stand up
pretty well on their own, Celerity is purely a helper discipline.
With Potence, Presence, Auspex, and so on it's fantastic.

But on it's own take a look:
Bleed: I'll Cat Burglary you to death (cough)
Bounce: Nope
Rush: None
Vote: Uh-Uh
Combat: Pretty Good, but can't really lay the smackdown without a
helper discipline or Weapons.

Variety is the spice of life, and Celerity is on a respirator..

>Which discipline do you find yourself playing the most? (not

Obfuscate. Not just for the stealth, but for the variety
it adds to any deck (Mask, Disguised Weapon, Memory's Fading
Glimpse, and so on).

> What are your opinions other than you disagree with mine?

That, in this instance, I fail to see that you have asserted a case for
why Auspex is weak - just that you can build decks to get around it. That
doesn't make Auspex weak, that just means that you can build specific
decks - a necessary skill, at times, especially if, say, your group finds
a specific deck type dominating. In these instances, it is often
necessary to build a deck type which clearly circumvents it (e.g. if
Fortitude excels in your group, use the Thaumaturgy cards to get round it,
if bleed excels, use a lot of bleed bounce - and so on). However, that a
specific counter exists for a deck or a discipline does not make that deck
or discipline intrinsically weak.

> What
> is your stance on the strongest and weakest disciplines?

I have already clearly stated that, in my opinion, Dominate is generally
voiced as the strongest discipline. This is a position I would tend to
agree with, though I can see why Fortitude is also a strong discipline
played mono. I believe, though, that Dominate, played in tandem with a
sensible discipline (e.g. presence, obfuscate etc. - something that
matches up in a clan and meshes well with Dominate), is probably superior.

> All I have
> seen you do is attack my position without voicing your own.

Again, I suggest you check your ISPs news-server, or your own news-reading
software. Clearly, one of them is at fault.

I have clearly stated that I believe Auspex to be a very,
very useful discipline, but not one I would use as a mono-discipline,and
most likely one I would use either for intercept combat, or for intercept
in a deck as a secondary discipline where intercept was needed. Further,
if you were playing someone like the Tremere, it could be useful for
bounce (though Dominate might be a better choice, depending on your
vampires). Similarly, the Toreador and Tzimisce (both clans which could
benefit from bleed bounce or reduction) can happily use them. The
Malkavians, too, though I tend to see a lot of dominate out with them
(naturally) so generally bleed bounce is good.

With regards actual weakest discipline, I can see many arguments in favour
of Thaumaturgy, but am not entirely certain.

In general, I tend to regard most mono-discipline decks as reasonably
shaky, though Dominate and Fortitude have some quite useful advantages.
As such, I tend to regard how well a discipline does when used to its best
advantage - with the right vampires, equipment, master cards, and so on.
(Potence, on its own, has truoble maneuvering, Auspex has trouble hitting
back once it has intercepted, Celerity can't really capitalise on the
excellent positions it can generate in combat. Working with a second
discipline helps here.)
